pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested

phonemes.desc: Written nt or n.t; conventionally vocalised “Neith”.
Feminine ending; the name may be a participle, “the terrible one” or “the weaver”.
The dot in the transliteration marks the feminine ending written with the water-ripple: the goddess’s name carries her own element.

pronunciation.note: One of Egypt’s oldest attested theonyms — her sign appears on Predynastic pottery.

domains.title: Goddess of Weaving, War, and the Primeval Waters
domains.subtitle: The Terrible One, Mother of the Gods
domains.lead: Nt — Neith — is Egypt’s primordial goddess: older than the Ennead, mistress of the arrows of war and the loom of creation, who wove the world’s fabric at Sais before the gods had names. The ancients called her “the great cow who bore the sun”, and made her the mother of Sobek, of the crocodiles, and of Ra himself in the oldest cosmogonic strand.

cards.name: The Weaver
cards.desc: Creator as textile-worker: she wove the world’s fabric on her loom at Sais.

cards.name: Mistress of the Bow
cards.desc: War-goddess whose arrows decide battles; her symbol is the crossed arrows on a shield.

cards.name: Mother of the Gods
cards.desc: Sole parent of Sobek in the Fayum tradition; in the Esna theology she bears the sun.

cards.name: Lady of Sais
cards.desc: Her city in the western Delta held her great temple and the mysteries of the primeval waters.

mythology.lead: Neith’s mythology is theology in the superlative: she is not a goddess within the pantheon but the condition of it. Her priesthood at Sais taught that she was self-generated, that she wove the world, and that all gods were her children — a doctrine so old it survived into the latest periods essentially unchanged.

myths.title: The Cow Who Bore the Sun
myths.text: The great hymns of Esna make Neith the mother of Ra: she as the celestial cow gives birth to the sun-disc from between her horns, and the seven scorpions that escort Isis are her daughters. Creation here is maternity on a cosmic scale — the goddess is the source from which the solar order proceeds.

myths.title: Mother of Sobek
myths.text: In the crocodile-god’s country, Neith is Sobek’s mother and the lady of the deep waters he rises from. The pairing of a primeval water-goddess with her crocodile son gives the Fayum’s theology its structure: she is the Nun-like depth, he its dangerous, fertile emergence.

myths.title: The Oracle of the Gods
myths.text: When the divine tribunal deadlocked over the succession of Horus and Seth, Neith was consulted as the eldest of counsel. Her written oracle — quoted verbatim in the New Kingdom narrative — demands the throne for Horus and compensation for Seth, and threatens to make the sky fall if the gods disobey. They obeyed.

myths.title: The Veiled Image of Sais
myths.text: Plutarch preserves the mystery of her cult-image at Sais: an image that was never unveiled, before which stood the inscription ‘I am all that has been, and is, and shall be; and no mortal has ever lifted my veil.’ The aisa-mysteries of Sais entered the Hermetic and Platonic imagination as the emblem of unknowable first-nature.

lore.syncretism: Neith merges with the great mother-goddesses — Mut, Hathor, Nut — and in the Roman period with Athena, whose war-and-craft profile fit her uncannily; the Greeks of Sais simply called her Athena. The identification was so natural that Herodotus describes her Sais temple in Athenian terms.
lore.culturalLegacy: Her Sais oracle became a proverb of ancient wisdom, quoted from Plutarch to the Renaissance Hermetica; ‘lifting the veil of Isis (Neith)’ passed into modern language as the image of unveiled nature. In Egyptology she anchors the study of Predynastic religion — her crossed-arrows sign is among the earliest divine emblems known.
lore.extendedMeditation: Nt is a name that predates the temples that housed it. Restoring it in plain letters is a kind of archaeological act: the further back a goddess stands, the fewer marks she needs. Her weaving metaphor survives every translation — the world as text, the text as fabric, the goddess as the first author of both.

sources.name: Esna temple hymns (the great Neith cosmogonies)
Contendings of Horus and Seth (Neith’s oracle)
Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (the veiled image of Sais)

lore.archaeology: Her Delta city Sais — biblical and classical Saïs — was the capital of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty, which consciously revived her archaic cult; its great temple is now largely lost to the water table, but the Esna inscriptions record its liturgy. The crossed-arrows emblem occurs from Naqada-period potsherds to Roman stelae.
lore.cult: The mysteries of Neith at Sais were among Egypt’s most secret rites; her priesthood was famously matrilineal in the late period, and the kings of Dynasty 26 took her name into their titulary to legitimise their Saïtic line. Her festival of the ‘Burning of the Lamps’ lit the temple through the night in mystery.
lore.iconography: A woman wearing the Deshret red crown of Lower Egypt, holding crossed arrows and a shield, or suckling the infant crocodiles — her Fayum maternity. In her primeval form she is the great cow whose body spans the sky, the sun between her horns.
lore.reception: Plutarch’s veiled inscription made her the ancient world’s favourite image of transcendent nature; Renaissance Neoplatonists, Enlightenment freemasonry and even the inscription on early geology societies borrowed ‘no mortal has lifted my veil’. She remains the standard example of a goddess whose cult outlived every dynasty that served her.
